after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{2}?$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =x \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =x\,i+y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-1,1),$ $(2,2),$ and $(2,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,1) & =-\,i+j \\ ∇f(2,2) & =2\,i+2\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =2\,i+(-1)j=2\,i-j\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062668/assets/369ebf19405768bcca19f4981f0237647836250548b0a33f9b4fdba92d85ddc9.png)

EXPLANATION

The gradient vector field of a function f is given by ∇f.

First, we find the partial derivatives: fx(x,y)=∂∂x(x2+y22)=xfy(x,y)=∂∂y(x2+y22)=y

So, the gradient vector field of f(x,y) is ∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=xi+yj.

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points (−1,1), (2,2), and (2,−1).

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for ∇f.

∇f(−1,1)=−i+j∇f(2,2)=2i+2j∇f(2,−1)=2i+(−1)j=2i−j

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}?$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & ={y}^{2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =2xy\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & ={y}^{2}\,i+2xy\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-2,1),$ $(2,1),$ and $(-2,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,1) & ={1}^{2}\,i+2\cdot (-2)\cdot 1\,j=i-4j \\ ∇f(2,1) & ={1}^{2}\,i+2\cdot 2\cdot 1\,j=i+4\,j \\ ∇f(-2,-1) & =(-1)^{2}\,i+2\cdot (-2)\cdot (-1)\,j=i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Which of the following could be the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y?$
after.worked_solution:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

- Setting $f(x,y)=-1,$ we get ${x}^{2}-y=-1,$ which gives the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1$

- Setting $f(x,y)=0,$ we get ${x}^{2}-y=0,$ that is, the parabola $y={x}^{2}$

- Setting $f(x,y)=2,$ we get ${x}^{2}-y=2,$ that is, the parabola $y={x}^{2}-2$

- $⋯$

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062668/assets/77a54ef31c41e0246e3d337a69c7faa161194058e6a5c672ef24d86866a83faf.png)

Note that $f(x,y)$ increases as we move downward and away from the origin $O.$ 

Now, we recall the following facts:

- The gradient field vectors of a function $f(x,y)$ always lie perpendicular to its level curves.

- Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where $f(x,y)$ increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062668/assets/4e124d5e77ef9a28002aba9aac40f0b7eff1232dd1c08b6bca10b166469675c7.png)

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062668/assets/8bd5b7575d1693935df0d25a259767f0dd267fc1153139cd55cebad75e3988fd.png)

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Which of the following could be the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}?$
after.worked_solution:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

- Setting $f(x,y)=0,$ we get $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=0,$ which gives the origin $O$

- Setting $f(x,y)=1,$ we get $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=1,$ which gives an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $1$ centered at $O$

- Setting $f(x,y)=4,$ we get $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=4,$ which gives an ellipse with semiaxes $4$ and $2$ centered at $O$

- $⋯$

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062668/assets/835b4206e04d064485d02635cfd4e2ad39a934b1d2b38296cc6463a265f5d931.png)

Note that $f(x,y)$ increases as we move away from the origin.

Now, we recall the following facts:

- The gradient field vectors of a function $f(x,y)$ always lie perpendicular to its level curves.

- Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where $f(x,y)$ increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062668/assets/cd8e0a10d162d30be895fa4ce49e3944e4e1a3ee9f79aa2fafe70c0edd2c0d61.png)

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:
